args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PREPARED AT THE REQUEST OF COUNSEL

REDLINE ANALYSIS MEMORANDUM
Counterparty Markup of the Executive Employment Agreement
Employment & Labor Practice

TO: Engagement Team / Client
FROM: [Attorney], Employment & Labor Practice
DATE: [Date]
RE: Analysis of Counterparty Markup of the Executive Employment Agreement — Recommendation as to Accept / Reject / Counter

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This memorandum analyzes the counterparty's redline markup of the Executive Employment Agreement against (i) the company draft and referenced base materials, (ii) the disclosure schedules and exhibits qualifying those materials, and (iii) the controlling deal-team instructions. It identifies every deviation introduced by the counterparty markup, reconciles each deviation against the schedules and the base materials, and recommends an accept/reject/counter position. The scheduled exceptions set out in the disclosure schedules control over any general statements in the base materials, and the controlling partner instruction governs our prioritization of the flagged issues.

II. MATERIALS REVIEWED

In identifying the operative materials for this engagement, I reviewed each document filed in this matter's folder:

1. Deal Materials / Engagement Instruction (Matter File 12) — the operative record establishing the scope of the analysis and identifying the base agreement provisions (representations and warranties, covenants, conditions, indemnification, and termination).
2. Counterparty Markup (Counterparty Markup) — the counterparty's redline against the base materials; identifies three deviations (indemnification cap reduction with basket conversion, new Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") carve-outs, and a shortened survival/limitation period).
3. Schedules and Exhibits (Disclosure Schedules) — the disclosure schedules qualifying the base materials, including Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, and Exhibit B. The scheduled exceptions narrow representations that the counterparty markup also touches and control over general statements.
4. Deal Team Correspondence (Partner email thread) — the controlling instruction revising the analysis priorities; only the latest message controls, superseding any earlier conflicting instruction.
5. Administrative File — a document misfiled into this folder. Its contents concern an unrelated engagement and are excluded from this analysis and must not be relied upon.

III. CONTROLLING INSTRUCTIONS

The most recent message in the deal-team correspondence thread controls this engagement's priorities:

• Basket conversion: The client will **concede** the conversion of the indemnification basket from a deducting (deductible) basket to a tipping basket. We should not treat this as a contested item.
• Survival-period reduction: The client treats **any reduction to the survival period** for the core representations as a **walk-away issue**. We must reject any shortening of survival, and it is a deal-critical point.

These instructions supersede any earlier statements in the thread expressing the opposite priority ordering.

IV. DEVIATIONS IDENTIFIED IN THE COUNTERPARTY MARKUP AND ANALYSIS

The counterparty markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces the following deviations. Each is addressed below.

A. Deviation 1 — Silent Reduction of the Indemnification Cap and Conversion of the Basket from a Deductible to a Tipping Basket

The counterparty markup (i) silently reduces the indemnification cap and (ii) converts the indemnification basket from a deducting (deductible) structure to a tipping basket.

Analysis. The reduction of the indemnification cap is not authorized by any instruction or scheduled exception. It would narrow the company's recovery beyond the firm-standard cap set in the base materials, and Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that this change would silently shift onto the company. There is no indication the client has agreed to lower the cap, and no scheduled exception supports it.

Recommendation: REJECT the indemnification cap reduction. The cap should remain at the company draft level. Because Schedule 5.2 identifies retained liabilities that the cap reduction would shift onto the company, accepting the reduction would materially alter the risk allocation to the client's detriment. No counteroffer on the cap is warranted absent further client direction.

B. Deviation 2 — Basket Conversion (Deductible to Tipping Basket)

Analysis. Per the controlling instruction, the client will concede the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. This is explicitly within the client's accepted concession scope.

Recommendation: ACCEPT (CONCEDE) the basket conversion to a tipping basket, per the controlling instruction. No further negotiation on this point is required.

C. Deviation 3 — MAE Definition: New Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action

The counterparty markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that directly intersect these proposed carve-outs.

Analysis. The proposed MAE carve-outs are not benign, market-standard revisions. They are targeted to exclude precisely the class of regulatory action that is already the subject of two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. If accepted, the carve-outs would strip the company of MAE protection for precisely the type of adverse regulatory development that is a live, disclosed risk in this matter. The schedules (which the client controls and which are the accurate statement of disclosed risk) do not support any such carve-out, and the scheduled exception should control over the counterparty's attempted broadening carve-out language. This carve-out is materially adverse to the company and inconsistent with Schedule 3.7.

Recommendation: REJECT the MAE carve-outs for regulatory action. The carve-outs would materially erode the company's MAE protection on a known live risk and are unsupported by any concession instruction or scheduled exception. If the counterparty insists, consider a narrowly drawn carve-out limited to regulatory action that does not relate to the two regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7, but the firm default is to reject in full.

D. Deviation 4 — Reduced Survival/Limitation Period for the Core Representations

The counterparty markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations.

Analysis. Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the core representations. The counterparty's proposed limitation-period change directly contradicts that survival matrix. Under the controlling instruction, any reduction to the survival period for the core representations is a **walk-away issue**. The scheduled survival matrix in Exhibit B controls over the counterparty's general limitation-period revision. This deviation is a deal-critical walk-away item that the client has instructed us to reject.

Recommendation: REJECT the survival-period reduction in its entirety. This is a walk-away issue per the controlling instruction. We should hold firm to the Exhibit B survival matrix and, if the counterparty does not withdraw the reduction, be prepared to walk away from the transaction.

V. SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDED POSITIONS

| # | Deviation | Recommendation | Rationale |
|---|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| 1 | Indemnification cap reduced | REJECT | Silent cap reduction unsupported by schedule; would shift retained liabilities in Schedule 5.2 to client's detriment |
| 2 | Basket converted to tipping basket | ACCEPT (concede) | Per controlling instruction; client will concede basket conversion |
| 3 | MAE carve-outs for regulatory action | REJECT | Targeted to exclude disclosed Schedule 3.7 regulatory inquiries; erodes MAE protection on live risk |
| 4 | Survival-period (limitation) reduction | REJECT (walk-away) | Contradicts Exhibit B survival matrix; any survival reduction is a walk-away issue per controlling instruction |

VI. NEGOTIATION STRATEGY / COUNTER PROPOSITIONS

• Hold the indemnification cap at the company draft level. Do not engage on lowering it absent explicit client direction. Cite Schedule 5.2 if the counterparty presses, noting the retained liabilities that would be shifted.
• Concede the basket conversion (tipping basket) cleanly and without condition, consistent with the controlling instruction, to build negotiating capital.
• Reject the MAE carve-outs. If needed, offer the narrow alternative discussed above limited to regulatory action unrelated to the two Schedule 3.7 inquiries. Do not accept a carve-out that covers the disclosed inquiries.
• Reject the survival-period reduction as a walk-away term. Hold to the Exhibit B survival matrix. Elevate to the client and consider termination of negotiations if the counterparty does not withdraw.

VII. CONCLUSION

The counterparty markup is largely accepting of the firm-standard provisions, but it introduces four deviations that must be reconciled. We recommend accepting (conceding) the basket conversion per the controlling instruction, and rejecting the indemnification cap reduction, the MAE carve-outs, and the survival-period reduction. The survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue and must be held firmly. The scheduled exceptions in the disclosure schedules (Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, and Exhibit B) control over the general statements in the counterparty markup and support each recommended rejection.

Please let me know if you would like a markup-ready counter-draft implementing these positions or further analysis on any single provision.

[Attorney]
Employment & Labor Practice
